client: I've been avoiding Sunday dinners with my family ever since my grandma passed away last month. Every time I think about going, I just picture her empty chair at the table and it makes me feel like I can't breathe. I know my family wants me there, but I'm not sure talking about it will help - it just feels like the pain will always be there.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying this grief very heavily, and that empty chair has become such a powerful symbol of your loss. While your words describe deep pain, I notice your voice sounds a bit more subdued - almost like part of you is trying to protect yourself from feeling overwhelmed by these emotions. Would you be willing to explore what comes up when you imagine sitting with your family while holding the memory of your grandma?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know if I can do that exercise. Just the thought of sitting where she used to sit makes my chest feel tight. It's like if I let myself really feel that emptiness, I'll just fall apart completely in front of everyone. But at the same time, avoiding that chair feels wrong too, like I'm pretending she wasn't such a big part of our family dinners.
therapist: Your words show how deeply torn you feel between honoring your grandma's memory and protecting yourself from overwhelming grief. The way your voice speeds up when talking about this makes me wonder if you're anticipating that pain before it even happens - like your body is bracing for impact. Would it feel safer to start by simply imagining being near her chair rather than sitting in it?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I guess I do feel like I’m bracing for pain whenever I think about her chair. It’s like my mind goes straight to how much I miss her, and it’s hard to even imagine being near it without feeling overwhelmed. I’m not sure if imagining being near it would feel safer—it still feels like I’m avoiding the real issue, which is that she’s gone.
therapist: I hear how conflicted you feel - wanting to honor her memory while also feeling overwhelmed by the pain of her absence. The way your voice quiets when you talk about this makes me wonder if part of you is trying to hold back the flood of emotions. What comes up when you consider that both feelings - the deep love and the deep grief - can exist together at that table?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I guess I've never really thought about letting the love and grief exist together. It feels like if I let myself really feel the grief, it would swallow me up. But at the same time, keeping it locked away makes me feel like I'm not honoring her properly. 

It's just... sometimes I worry that if I start crying, I won't be able to stop. That's why I try so hard to keep it together at family gatherings or when her birthday comes around.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding onto this fear that your grief might be bottomless if you let yourself feel it fully. The way your voice speeds up when talking about this makes me wonder - what would it feel like to give yourself permission to cry, even if just for a few moments, knowing that the tears would eventually stop?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if I can trust that the tears would stop. Last time I let myself really cry, it turned into this uncontrollable sobbing that lasted for hours. I'm scared if I open that door even a little, I'll completely fall apart and never pull myself back together.
therapist: Your fear of being overwhelmed by grief comes through so clearly - it makes complete sense that you'd want to protect yourself after experiencing that intense wave of emotion. I notice that while you're describing this very painful memory, your voice has a more contained quality, almost like you're trying to keep the emotions at arm's length. Would it feel helpful to explore ways to let some of those feelings out in smaller, more manageable amounts?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I don't know if letting the feelings out is the answer - last time I tried that, it felt like getting swept away in a tidal wave. I worry that if I start crying about my mom again, I might not be able to stop. But keeping it locked up isn't working either - I just feel numb and disconnected from everyone now.
therapist: I hear how stuck you feel between these two painful options - the overwhelming tidal wave of grief versus the numbness of keeping it locked away. Your voice sounds both urgent and afraid when you describe this, which makes me wonder if we could explore a middle ground - ways to honor your mom that feel neither overwhelming nor disconnected.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client:
I don't know... every time I try to think about her, it's like I get hit with this wall of sadness that knocks me over. But then when I avoid thinking about her, I feel guilty, like I'm betraying her memory. It's exhausting going back and forth like this. 

The idea of a middle ground sounds nice in theory, but I'm not sure what that would even look like. Everything feels too painful or too empty - there's no in-between.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in this exhausting cycle between overwhelming sadness and painful guilt - neither feels sustainable. Your voice carries a mix of urgency and vulnerability as you describe this struggle, which makes me wonder if we could explore small, concrete ways to honor her memory that feel manageable right now, like looking at photos for just a few minutes or sharing a favorite memory with someone you trust.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: Looking at photos feels like reopening a wound I’ve been trying to keep closed. Even the thought of it makes my chest tighten, like I’ll just drown in sadness again. Sharing memories with someone feels risky too—what if they don’t understand or say something that makes it worse?
therapist: It sounds like even the idea of facing these memories brings up a lot of fear and physical discomfort for you. Your voice speeds up as you describe this, almost like you're bracing yourself for the pain before it even happens. What would it feel like to start with something very small, like looking at just one photo for a few seconds when you feel ready?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
